source.title: We Inspected Every Head In GPT-2 Small using SAEs So You Don’t Have To
source.authors: robertzk; Connor Kissane; Arthur Conmy; Neel Nanda

record.tranche_reason: It uses SAE feature attribution and synthetic induction tests to examine induction-head behavior, rather than reproducing the original training-time measurements.
record.gate_note: The post reports induction-head identifications and experiments on synthetic and sampled training-distribution examples. It does not measure induction-head formation over training, token-index in-context-learning loss, or the role of induction heads in broad few-shot task learning. Some referenced plots have no numerical values in the supplied text; only their accompanying textual descriptions are recorded.
record.test_reason: The post identifies heads with induction behaviour in GPT-2 Small, and reports signs of them in GPT-2 Medium. It uses SAE attribution, synthetic repeated-token data, DLA and corruption tests. That is a result on V4 universality in a new setting. It does not study attention-only models, previous-token composition, training dynamics or in-context-learning loss.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that per-head SAE attribution recovers known GPT-2 Small heads, including induction and previous-token heads, and that most heads (>90%) are polysemantic. It also motivated the hypothesis, confirmed with non-SAE experiments, that H5.1 does long-prefix induction while H5.5 does standard induction. They see hints of universality in GPT-2 Medium.
record.recipe_differences: Uses attention-layer SAE feature attribution and synthetic induction examples, plus direct-logit-attribution and corrupted-example checks. It does not reproduce the original training-time phase-change and in-context-learning-loss measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported distinction between H5.1 and H5.5 depends on prefix length: H5.1 changes sharply in the long-prefix regime, while H5.5 is described as relatively constant.

fits_no_version.finding: The two Layer 5 induction heads in GPT-2 Small specialize. H5.1 does long-prefix induction (needs at least 2 matching prefix tokens); H5.5 does standard one-token induction. On corrupted examples, H5.1's induction score falls from ~0.55 to ~0.05.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Induction heads in a model divide labour by prefix-match length (long-prefix vs standard induction).

record.problems: Induction-head interpretation partly relies on the top 10 SAE features and decoder-weight attribution, which the authors call an imperfect proxy; they recommend FVE for reproductions. The post says the head investigations were shallow. No uncertainty estimates or sample sizes are given for the case-study results, and the supplied text ambiguously attributes both long-prefix and one-prefix behavior to H5.1 in one passage.

untested.parts: All of V1: no attention-only models, no previous-token-head composition test. Previous-token head 4.11 is only identified, not linked to the induction heads.

missing.what: Further heads flagged with partial or non-standard induction: H9.9 (copying names, some induction) and H10.10 (possibly non-standard induction). Also, the SAE method recovered only 2 of the 3 known induction heads in layers 5-6.
missing.locator: Overview of Attention Heads Across Layers, layer table rows 6, 9, 10

record.verdict_notes: Rows were relinked from V1 to V4 because GPT-2 Small is not attention-only and composition with a previous-token head is not tested. A typo in the training-distribution and corruption passages names H5.1 for both heads, which makes r11 and r13 unreadable. The prefix-length 'phase change' is unrelated to V2. Evidence is mostly qualitative, with no uncertainty or sample sizes. Alignment Forum post, not peer reviewed.

versions.untested_parts: The post does not test whether induction heads form by composing with an earlier previous-token head, and it does not study attention-only transformers. It tests induction behavior in GPT-2 Small and reports a GPT-2 Medium result.
Formation over training, a narrow early-training window, a coincident in-context-learning gain, and a training-loss bump.
Whether induction heads account for most token-index in-context learning or few-shot learning in large transformers.
The post reports signs in GPT-2 Medium in addition to its GPT-2 Small study, but does not test other model families, multiple training runs, other architectures, or other modalities.
Whether training data or training setup affects head formation or the persistence of in-context learning. The reported corruption changes evaluation examples, not the model's training.
Whether few-shot task learning mainly uses mechanisms other than induction heads.
Whether induction-head formation comprises multiple training transitions or sub-steps.

source_check.notes: The source repeats H5.1 for both sides of two comparisons, apparently typographical errors; do not silently assign the ~0.45 comparator to H5.5. For r7, relative constancy is acceptable only as a comparison with H5.1: both induction scores rise, while explicit constancy concerns H5.5's DLA.

statements.correction: GPT-2 Small: both heads' synthetic induction scores increase with prefix length; H5.1 increases much more dramatically at prefix lengths >=2. H5.1 DLA rises sharply; H5.5 DLA remains relatively constant. Corrupting training-distribution long-prefix examples to one-prefix examples reduces H5.1's average induction score from ~0.55 to ~0.05. Comparator score: ~0.45; printed head identifier: H5.1, apparently a typo. Numeric prefix-length endpoints: not stated. The stated 0.3 is an example-filtering threshold.
statements.problem: The prefix-length endpoints <0.3, >0.7 and 0.7 are not stated in the text. The corruption comparator is ~0.45, not 0.43, and the source labels it H5.1 again, leaving its attribution ambiguous. The qualitative prefix dependence and H5.1 corruption result are supported.
